[ITQAN:v2p334#2/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | لو تدهن means “if you compromise or relax your position with them, they will compromise in return.”
[ITQAN:v2p582/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some explain the reading ودوا لو تدهن فيدهنوا as equivalent in meaning to أن تدهن.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Persian admonitory verse says that words without deeds are false, a sleeper cannot awaken another sleeper, and counsel must be heard attentively.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The opponents, immersed in vice and shifting desires, flatter in turn and add this vice to their others, hoping the Prophet will reciprocate their compromise.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم | reports | Some distinguish blameworthy mudāhana, selling religion for worldly gain, from praiseworthy mudārā, giving up worldly interest for religion.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r12] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي | reports | A Prophetic saying that he was commanded to show courteous accommodation to people, just as he was commanded to convey the message, does not license improper compromise.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r13] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الإمام الغزالي | reports | Al-Ghazālī says the motive for overlooking a fault distinguishes the two: overlooking to protect religion or reform one's brother is mudārā; doing so for self-interest, desires, or status is mudāhana.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r14] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو الدرداء | reports | Abū al-Dardāʾ says one may smile in the faces of people while the heart condemns them; Bursevī presents this as courteous accommodation toward someone whose harm is feared.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Once the foregoing is clear, the Prophet must persist in refusing their demand that he stop confronting them; he is ordered to stand firm despite his small following and their large numbers.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verse shows that obeying a disobedient person is itself disobedience, and yielding to a tyrant is transgression.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Law is optative here; idhān, originally akin to oiling and derived from oil, means leniency, accommodation, or abandoning a firm position.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Their hoped-for response is that they would then refrain from attacking or criticizing the Prophet.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | On one parsing, fa coordinates yad-hinūna with the optative clause, so it stays indicative rather than losing nūn as a subjunctive result.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | Alternatively, fa marks consequence: they would accommodate him as a result of his accommodating them; the verb can also describe their present flattery in hope of his compromise.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الكاشفي | reports | Al-Kāshifī paraphrases the verse as a refusal to obey polytheists who invite the Prophet to his forefathers' religion; they want him to soften his criticism of their idolatry so they will reciprocate and stop taunting his faith.
[BURSEVI:v10p83#3/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم | reports | Some advise that outward conduct should agree with inward conviction; outward compliance without inward agreement becomes fleeting hypocrisy and dissimulation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p26#3/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | They wish the Prophet would soften and accommodate them in some matters.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p26#3/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The result may mean they would then compromise too, or that they already compromise in hope of inducing him to do so; the ف introduces the resulting clause.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p26#3/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alternatively, فيدهنون coordinates with تدهن inside the scope of لو: they wish to compromise after he does, with sequence occurring in their wish; al-Alusi calls the preceding parses more remote amid the disputed analyses.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p26#3/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · هارون | reports | Some codices, as Harun reports, read فيدهنوا without the indicative ن; it may be subjunctive as the response to the wish or coordinated under a reading of لو as نصب-producing أن.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p26#3/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · جمهور النحاة | reports | Most grammarians keep لو in its ordinary conditional sense, with an omitted apodosis and object of ودوا: they would be pleased if he compromised and then they would do so.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p26#3/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Their compromise means showing softness while concealing the opposite; in their wish for the Prophet only outward softness counts, since they detest his concealing a contrary view.
[ELMALILI:68:7-33#2/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The deniers called the Prophet deluded or misguided out of malice and wished him to flatter them by leaving their idols and injustices unchallenged; had he accommodated them, they would have flattered and affirmed his falsehoods.
[ELMALILI:68:7-33#2/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The first foundation of noble character is to refuse obedience to the deniers and avoid flattering their aims; compromising tongues and pens are far from moral greatness and reason.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p68/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الكلبي وزيد بن أسلم والحسن | reports | Al-Kalbī, Zayd ibn Aslam, and al-Ḥasan report that the polytheists wanted the Prophet to stop publicly denouncing them so they would stop harming him and both sides could accommodate each other.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p68/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Waddū means that they loved or wished for this accommodation.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p68/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The wish is not merely private desire disclosed to the Prophet, since that would not fit the command not to obey the deniers.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p68/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · كتب السيرة | reports | Sira books say the polytheists made the Prophet such an offer through his uncle Abū Ṭālib and ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p68/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The offer followed the opening verses’ warning: they could stop calling him mad if he stopped humiliating their idols and forebears, leaving each side to its worship. | mentions 68:5, 68:6, 68:7, 68:51
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The fāʾ can suggest why they wanted accommodation: they themselves are accommodating, and people with bad intentions want others to resemble them.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The wish clause explains what the forbidden obedience would consist of, so it is set apart rather than coordinated.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Tudhin derives from idhān, accommodation or ingratiating softness; literally, applying oil softens or colors something, from which its figurative senses developed, as al-Rāghib notes.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | They wished the Prophet would accommodate them so they would reciprocate with good treatment.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The fāʾ links the response to “if you accommodate” and explains the consequence or cause of their wish; it does not make the following verb su

bjunctive.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | An omitted nominal subject, “then they,” precedes the verbal predicate; this fronting restricts accommodation to them and tells the Prophet not to adopt it.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Law may be conditional, with tudhin as the condition and an omitted result: if the Prophet accommodated them, they would get what they wanted.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الفراء والفارسي والتبريزي وابن مالك | reports | Al-Farrāʾ, al-Fārisī, al-Tabrīzī, and Ibn Mālik allow law to function as a verbal noun particle like an, yielding “they wished for your accommodation.”
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p69/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The object of waddū is omitted and understood from law tudhin, or it is the verbal noun if law is treated as a maṣdariyya particle.
[TABATABAI:68:1-33#2/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The deniers want the Prophet to soften his religion by drawing near to them, so they will reciprocate by compromising theirs; the author understands the desire as covering both parts of the phrase and the fa as elaborating consequence.
[TABATABAI:68:1-33#2/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | One reported proposal was that the Prophet stop mentioning their idols and they would leave him and his Lord alone.
[ASAD-NOTES:68:7#n5/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · Asad | holds | The opponents want ethical and moral concessions from the Prophet, promising to reciprocate and stop actively opposing him.
[BINTSHATI:v2p54/r7] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | Idhān means softness, leniency, or accommodation; mudāhana is evasive compromise or disingenuous appeasement.
[BINTSHATI:v2p54/r8] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | The root relates to oil used to soften or smooth: dahān is dye or paint, and dahīn describes a slippery place as if oiled.
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r1] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | The Qur’an’s literal oil-related sense of d-h-n appears in the examples from al-Muʾminūn and al-Raḥmān. | mentions 23:20, 55:37
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r10] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | The author distinguishes idhān, the metaphor of softening speech, from mudāhana, which can mean accommodation and ingratiation.
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r11] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | The particle law conveys the opponents’ remote, frustrated wish; exegetes and grammarians instead fixated on the retained nūn in fayudhinūna and its inflectional rule.
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r2] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | Idhān derives from oil and figuratively means softening or lenience, as softening speech resembles softening oil.
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r3] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | Mudāhana commonly describes ingratiation or cajoling involving deceit, or laxity and dereliction.
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r4] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | The metaphorical sense of idhān also occurs in al-Wāqiʿa 56:81, alongside this verse. | mentions 56:81
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r5] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · قيل | reports | One reported gloss is that the opponents wanted Muhammad to make concessions so they would reciprocate with concessions.
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r6] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · قيل | reports | Another gloss is that they wished him to soften his religion so they would soften theirs.
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r7] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · قيل | reports | A further gloss is that they wanted him to lean toward their gods and abandon the truth, so they could accommodate him.
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r8] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · الطبري | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī prefers the reading that they wished Muhammad to compromise in religion by leaning toward their gods, after which they would accommodate his worship of God. | mentions 17:74
[BINTSHATI:v2p55/r9] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | reports | Al-Ṭabarī adduces 17:74, where Muhammad nearly leaned slightly toward the opponents, as support for his interpretation. | mentions 17:74
[BINTSHATI:v2p56/r1] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | reports | Traditional grammar makes the verb subjunctive after a wish because waddu law carries the sense of layta.
[BINTSHATI:v2p56/r2] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari accounts for the indicative wording by supplying a deleted predicate or reading it as a verbal noun construction.
[BINTSHATI:v2p56/r3] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | reports | Some codices reportedly read yudhinū without the nūn, with grammarians analyzing it either as a wish’s subjunctive response or as if an were spoken.
[BINTSHATI:v2p56/r4] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · أبو حيان | reports | Abu Hayyan says the majority of codices retain the nūn.
[BINTSHATI:v2p56/r5] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | prefers | The author says revelation is the grammatical authority: the fāʾ coordinates yudhinūn with tudhinu, keeping the indicative nūn and the causal nuance.
[BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p161/r1] BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 · author | holds | The opening verses affirm the Prophet’s mission and steady him against deniers who dispute the miracle and claim the Qur’an is merely tales of the ancients.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p427/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The opponents want Muhammad to soften his position so they can make reciprocal concessions; their opposition is bargaining against desire, not sincere commitment to religion.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p427/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The verse’s syntax suppresses the inchoative; the full sense is “they too will soften,” after the Prophet softens his stance.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:68:8/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | The unbelievers wanted the Prophet to compromise moral and spiritual principles and abandon Islamic teachings that conflicted with their interests, promising reciprocal concessions and noninterference.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:68:8/r3] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Şevkânî | reports | They proposed that the Prophet worship their idols for a time and they worship Allah, his God, for a time.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:68:8/r4] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | God requires the Prophet to remain firm without slackening: God's path is right, and truth cannot be mixed with falsehood.
[STUDYQURAN:68:9/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Dāhana can mean “to demean,” “to deny,” or “to take something lightly.”
[STUDYQURAN:68:9/r2] STUDYQURAN · author | reports | One reading has the disbelievers ready to compromise if the Prophet and his followers compromise; another has them already compromising and wanting believers to do likewise.
[STUDYQURAN:68:9/r3] STUDYQURAN · Bg | reports | On the first reading, disbelievers would trade concessions in religion or take turns worshipping one another’s gods.
[STUDYQURAN:68:9/r4] STUDYQURAN · Bg | reports | On the second reading, the disbelievers want believers to become disbelievers too.
